1999-06-28: Enron's board of directors approved the LJM1 off-balance-sheet partnership controlled by CFO Andy Fastow, waiving the company's ethics policy.
2001-04-17: Enron chairman Ken Lay privately met with Vice President Dick Cheney to offer suggestions for Cheney's energy task force and lobby against price caps in California.
2001-08-14: Jeff Skilling resigned as Enron's chief executive officer.
2001-10-12: A lawyer at Arthur Andersen ordered the destruction of thousands of documents related to Enron, raising questions of obstruction of justice amid the energy company's collapse.
2001-10-23: Enron CEO Ken Lay held a conference call with investors and analysts to explain the company's troubles as its stock price fell sharply, admitting an "inherent conflict of interest" in the CFO's partnerships with Enron.
2001-11-08: Enron confirmed it was in talks with smaller rival Dynegy over a takeover that could force the sale of its main British assets.
2001-11-29: Enron’s share price collapsed and its trading activity fell sharply after Dynegy withdrew from a merger deal that might have saved the company.
2001-11-30: Enron's collapse results in 1,100 of 1,400 UK staff losing their jobs as administrators from PricewaterhouseCoopers inform employees at the company's European headquarters in London.
2001-12-02: Enron believes its accounts may need further downward revision, making a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing this week almost certain.
Enron files for bankruptcy, the biggest in US history.
2001-12-04: Electricité de France expresses interest in buying Enron Direct, the European retail arm of failed US energy giant Enron.
Centrica acquires Enron Direct, the British retail arm of collapsed US energy trading company Enron, for £96.4m in cash.
2001-12-06: Enron paid $55m in bonuses to 500 staff while under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, sparking outrage among laid-off workers and creditors.
2001-12-12: Enron's chief financial officer outlined a plan to raise $6bn from asset sales, including Azurix and businesses in developing markets, as part of a strategy to emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection within a year.
2002-01-09: The US Justice Department launches a criminal investigation into the financial collapse of Enron, creating a task force to examine the energy giant.
2002-01-12: The collapse of Enron raises political concerns for the Bush administration over its ties to the company, including campaign contributions and meetings with executives.
2002-01-13: Article profiles key players in the Enron scandal, including former chairman and CEO Kenneth Lay, former president and CEO Jeffrey Skilling, and former CFO Andrew Fastow, amid investigations by Senate subcommittees and the SEC.
2002-01-14: The inquiry into Enron's collapse focuses on auditor Arthur Andersen and an October 12 memo ordering the destruction of potentially incriminating documents, as evidence grows of a cover-up.
2002-01-15: Sherron Watkins was revealed to the world as the Enron whistleblower who had warned chairman Kenneth Lay of major accounting irregularities months before the company collapsed into bankruptcy.
2002-01-17: Bankrupt Enron fired its longtime auditor Arthur Andersen amid recriminations over the destruction of financial documents.
Arthur Andersen confirmed holding discussions about whether to retain Enron as a client nine months before Enron filed for bankruptcy.
2002-01-22: A former Enron executive claims that documents were being shredded at the company's Houston headquarters as recently as last week, including material apparently connected to controversial partnerships, amid federal investigations into the bankrupt energy company.
2002-01-23: Kenneth Lay announced his resignation as chairman and chief executive of Enron amid criminal, congressional, and regulatory investigations into the company's financial meltdown.
2002-01-25: Former Enron vice-chairman John Clifford Baxter was found dead in a parked car in a Houston suburb from a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head, later ruled a suicide by a Texas coroner.
2002-01-31: Credit Suisse Group warns of a sharp fall in 2001 profits, partly due to $126 million in losses stemming from the meltdown of Enron.
2002-02-03: Downing Street failed to disclose a number of meetings between collapsed energy giant Enron and ministers and key advisers to Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, deepening the row over the company's influence.
2002-02-04: A US Senate committee cancels an Enron hearing after former chairman Kenneth Lay decides at the last minute not to appear.

Congress declared its intention to subpoena former Enron chief executive Kenneth Lay after he failed to appear at the first day of congressional hearings into Enron's collapse, and he stepped down from Enron's board.
2002-02-05: The Senate commerce committee subpoenas former Enron chairman Kenneth Lay to testify after he abruptly cancelled a scheduled congressional appearance, though his attorney says he cannot accept the subpoena partly because he does not know Lay's whereabouts.
2002-02-12: Former Enron chairman Kenneth Lay appeared before Congress under subpoena but declined to testify on Fifth Amendment grounds, as senators criticized him over Enron's collapse.
2002-02-13: Investigators trying to sift through the wreckage of Enron have identified two figures, Ben Glisan and Michael Kopper, they believe can help break the case.
2002-02-14: Enron whistleblower Sherron Watkins testified to a Congressional inquiry that company executives engaged in "sheer income statement manipulation" to hide losses from shareholders, and Enron fired two top accounting officers.

Enron whistleblower Sherron Watkins testified before Congress, blaming former CFO Andrew Fastow and former CEO Jeffrey Skilling for the company's accounting scandal and suggesting former chairman Kenneth Lay had been misled.
2002-02-15: About 100 Enron energy traders stand to receive commission payments of up to £24m to help administrators unwind the collapsed company's complex trading book, as creditors meet in London.
2002-02-16: Enron shareholders are preparing to file a lawsuit against major Wall Street banks, including Goldman Sachs, Salomon Smith Barney, and JP Morgan Chase, accusing their analysts of recommending Enron shares to secure lucrative work from the collapsed energy trader.
2002-02-17: Journalist Bethany McLean signs a seven-figure book deal with Penguin Books to write an account of the Enron scandal.
2002-02-18: Enron shareholders threaten to sue Wall Street investment banks for allegedly continuing to recommend Enron shares while the company headed toward collapse.
2002-02-26: Former Enron vice-president Sherron Watkins told the Senate commerce committee that CEO Kenneth Lay failed to act on her warnings about financial irregularities before the company's collapse.
Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling denied lying to Congress and duping chairman Kenneth Lay during Senate hearings on the energy firm's collapse.
2002-03-01: The focus on Wall Street's role in the Enron debacle shifts to Credit Suisse First Boston, which handed documents relating to its dealings with Enron to congressional investigators.
Enron rewarded its top executives with at least $320m in bonuses last year, payments now being scrutinized by federal investigators.
2002-04-03: US financial regulators have begun an unprecedented crackdown on accounting fraud with a near-threefold increase in investigations so far this year following the collapse of Enron.
2002-04-08: Barclays and other top financial institutions are added to an expanded class action lawsuit in connection with the Enron collapse.
2002-04-11: Police released the suicide note of former Enron vice-chairman John Clifford Baxter, who killed himself in January, revealing his despair and providing no further clue to Enron's collapse.
2002-04-12: Enron's chief executive Stephen Cooper told employees that legal claims against the bankrupt company could reach $100bn and warned of further job losses.
2002-05-08: The SEC upgrades its inquiry into Dynegy's natural gas supply deal to a full-scale investigation, amid scrutiny following Enron's collapse.
2002-05-14: Former Andersen partner David Duncan testified that the accounting firm considered dropping Enron as a client in February 2001 due to concerns about the energy firm's aggressiveness, and that he obstructed justice by instructing staff to destroy Enron audit documents.
2002-06-17: Enron disclosed it paid $681m to 140 top executives in the year leading up to its bankruptcy on December 2, 2001.
2002-07-08: Former Enron executive Kyran Hanks is appointed to a year-long post as director of gas trading arrangements at UK energy regulator Ofgem.
The Bank for International Settlements blamed Enron's collapse on a catastrophic failure of corporate governance.
2002-08-06: Federal prosecutors are investigating whether Enron may have bribed foreign government officials to win contracts for its international oil, gas and water businesses.
2002-08-21: Former Enron executive Michael Kopper pleads guilty to money laundering and wire fraud and agrees to cooperate with prosecutors, marking the first conviction in the case against Enron.
2002-08-28: Enron put its most valuable assets up for sale, moving toward a possible break-up that could mean the company ceases to exist.
2002-10-02: Former Enron chief financial officer Andrew Fastow was charged with three counts of fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy and surrendered to authorities in Houston.
2002-10-07: A Senate committee accuses the SEC of "systemic and catastrophic failure" in regulating Enron, claiming it failed to detect dubious practices and had not inspected any of Enron's annual reports since 1997.
2002-10-11: Abbey National files an $80m lawsuit against seven Wall Street banks to recover losses related to failed US energy trader Enron.
2002-10-17: Former top Enron energy trader Timothy Belden is expected to plead guilty to conspiring to commit fraud in the alleged ramping of electricity prices during the California energy crisis.
2002-11-15: Enron executive and whistleblower Sherron Watkins left the company to advise corporations on ethical issues.
2003-02-14: Enron used offshore special purpose entities and partnerships, including Mahonia, to borrow billions of dollars through prepaid swaps and keep debt off its books.
2003-03-06: Legal experts said a report builds the case against former senior Enron staff who have yet to be charged, as the investigation into the Enron scandal continues.
A bankruptcy court-appointed report concluded that Enron may have improperly transferred up to $5bn in assets and set the stage for a battle in the company's bankruptcy case.
2003-03-12: Two former Enron broadband division executives, Kevin Howard and Michael Krautz, were arrested and charged with faking $111 million in profits from a joint venture with Blockbuster.
2003-05-01: The US justice department announced new fraud and other criminal charges against former Enron chief financial officer Andrew Fastow, his wife Lea Fastow, and seven other ex-Enron officials in connection with the company's collapse.
2003-07-11: Enron submitted a bankruptcy reorganization plan under which most creditors would receive 14.4 to 18.3 cents on the dollar and the company would be divided into two new separate companies.
2003-08-20: Enron Corp, the bankrupt energy trading company, is seeking a buyer for its 50-storey Houston headquarters, appointing Granite Partners to handle the sale with bids due by September 19.
2003-09-10: Former Enron treasurer Ben Glisan was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty to criminal conspiracy, becoming the first executive jailed in the Enron scandal.
2003-10-30: Former Enron executive David Delainey pleaded guilty to criminal charges and settled SEC allegations, paying $8m in penalties and disgorgement over his role in falsifying Enron's earnings statements.
2003-11-24: A bankruptcy court-appointed examiner's report concluded that former Enron bosses Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling breached their fiduciary duty by failing to properly supervise special purpose entities used to hide Enron's debts and inflate its profits.
2004-01-07: Former Enron finance chief Andrew Fastow was negotiating a plea bargain for his role in the accounting scandal that brought down the energy firm.
2004-01-08: Former Enron finance chief Andrew Fastow is set to change his plea from innocent to guilty to fraud charges as part of a plea bargain, according to reports.
2004-01-14: Former Enron finance chief Andrew Fastow pleaded guilty to criminal fraud charges and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors in return for a 10-year prison sentence.
2004-01-22: Former Enron chief accounting officer Richard Causey surrendered to authorities and was indicted on five counts of securities fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud stemming from the energy firm's collapse.
2004-02-19: Former Enron chief executive Jeff Skilling was charged with 42 counts of fraud, insider trading, and giving false statements to auditors in a federal indictment.
2004-04-07: A plea deal with Lea Fastow, former Enron assistant treasurer and wife of former finance chief Andrew Fastow, collapsed when she withdrew her guilty plea after the judge refused to accept a five-month sentence, potentially jeopardizing Andrew Fastow's plea deal in the Enron fraud prosecution.
2004-05-06: Lea Fastow, wife of former Enron finance chief Andrew Fastow, is jailed for a year after pleading guilty to helping her husband hide ill-gotten gains from Enron-related financial schemes.
2004-06-27: Former Enron chief executive Kenneth Lay, speaking out for the first time since the company's collapse, denied wrongdoing and blamed finance chief Andrew Fastow for the firm's failure.
2004-07-02: Bank of America agrees to a $69m settlement in a class action lawsuit brought by Enron investors over alleged links to fraudulent activities before Enron's 2001 collapse.
2004-07-07: A Texas grand jury indicts former Enron chairman Ken Lay on charges related to the earnings inflation fraud that destroyed the company.
2004-07-08: The US justice department charged former Enron chairman Kenneth Lay with 11 counts, including conspiracy to commit securities fraud, making false and misleading statements, and bank fraud.
2004-09-20: The first criminal trial involving former Enron executives begins in Houston, with six defendants charged with conspiracy and fraud over a Nigerian barge deal.
2004-11-18: Enron cancelled its nearly worthless stock and completed the sale of its largest remaining assets as its court-approved bankruptcy plan became effective.
2005-03-23: UK Home Secretary Charles Clarke delays until May 24 a decision on a US request by Enron prosecutors to extradite three former NatWest bankers accused of conspiring to defraud the bank of $20m.
2005-04-21: Two former Merrill Lynch bankers were sentenced to prison for their roles in the Enron scandal.
2005-06-10: Citigroup agreed to pay $2bn to settle a lawsuit brought by Enron investors over the energy firm's collapse.
2005-06-15: JP Morgan Chase agrees to pay $2.2bn to the University of California and other investors following the collapse of Enron.
2005-08-02: Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce agrees to pay $2.4bn to settle a lawsuit brought by former Enron investors, the largest settlement so far stemming from Enron's collapse.
2005-08-16: JP Morgan Chase agreed to pay $1bn to settle claims brought against it by Enron, bringing the total cost of the bank's brush with the energy firm to $3.2bn.
2005-12-28: Former Enron chief accountant Richard Causey pleaded guilty to a single charge of securities fraud in exchange for a seven-year sentence, agreeing to cooperate with prosecutors against former chief executives Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling.
2006-01-23: The trial of former Enron chiefs Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling on 42 counts of conspiracy, fraud and insider trading is due to begin.
2006-01-30: The fraud trial of former Enron chairman Ken Lay and chief executive Jeff Skilling began with jury selection in Houston, with both denying 42 charges related to the company's collapse.
2006-01-31: Prosecutors opened their fraud case against former Enron chairman Ken Lay and former chief executive Jeff Skilling in a Houston courtroom, telling the jury the case is "not about the accounting but about the lies."
2006-03-07: Former Enron finance chief Andrew Fastow testified against former boss Jeffrey Skilling at the trial of Enron's two highest-ranking executives, describing off-balance-sheet entities used to hide debt and inflate profits.
2006-03-08: Former Enron CFO Andrew Fastow admitted to being "extremely greedy" during cross-examination in the trial of former bosses Jeffrey Skilling and Kenneth Lay, while claiming there was a "culture of corruption" at Enron.
2006-03-09: Former Enron finance director Andrew Fastow admitted he has no written evidence tying former chief executive Jeffrey Skilling to the financial vehicles used to manipulate earnings.
2006-03-15: Former Enron executive Sherron Watkins testified at the trial of Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling about her whistleblowing memo warning of accounting scandals and her discovery that managers had considered sacking her.
2006-04-10: Former Enron chief Jeffrey Skilling testified in a Houston court, denying knowledge of secret side deals and illegal activity at Enron.
2006-04-12: Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling, on trial for fraud and conspiracy over Enron's collapse, accused Wall Street analyst Richard Grubman of being part of a short-selling ring that spread rumors and disinformation to talk down the company's stock.
2006-04-15: Documents disclosed by prosecutors in the Enron fraud trial show that former Enron director Lord Wakeham brushed aside whistleblower Sherron Watkins's warnings about the company's finances two months before Enron filed for bankruptcy.
2006-04-23: Former Enron chief Kenneth Lay testified in his fraud trial that his pursuit of the American dream had ended in an "American nightmare" after the company's 2001 collapse.
2006-05-01: Enron founder Kenneth Lay ended six days of trial testimony, denying fraud charges and blaming the company's collapse on bad publicity and market loss of confidence.
2006-05-17: The Houston jury in the Enron trial began its deliberations over whether Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling were guilty of fraud.
2006-05-25: A jury finds Enron founder Kenneth Lay and former chief executive Jeffrey Skilling guilty of fraud and conspiracy.
2006-07-05: Kenneth Lay, the founder of Enron, died of a heart attack at his holiday home in Aspen, Colorado, at age 64, after being found guilty of fraud and conspiracy in May.
2006-07-14: US prosecutors seek a seven-to-nine-year jail sentence if the NatWest Three are convicted in an Enron-related fraud case, with former Enron executives Andrew Fastow and Michael Kopper providing evidence against them.
2006-08-07: The NatWest Three were served with subpoenas requiring them to give evidence in a class action brought by Enron shareholders who lost more than $40bn when the company collapsed.
2006-09-11: A radio program features former Enron accountant Sherron Watkins recounting her whistleblowing story five years after Enron's collapse in the biggest bankruptcy in American history.
2006-09-25: Former Enron chief financial officer Andrew Fastow was sentenced to six years in prison, reduced from the 10 years he had agreed to in a 2004 plea bargain, for his role in the scandal that bankrupted the company.
2006-10-22: Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling was sentenced to 24 years and four months in jail for his role in the energy company's fraud-riddled financial dealings that collapsed in one of America's biggest corporate scandals.
2006-10-23: Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling is sentenced for his role in the corporate scandal, facing at least 20 years in jail.
2006-10-24: Kenneth Lay, former Enron chief executive, had died of a heart attack in July at age 64, and his fraud and conspiracy convictions were thrown out after his death because he was unable to appeal.
Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling is sentenced to 24 years in prison for corporate fraud related to Enron's collapse.
2006-11-03: Barclays agrees to pay $144 million to settle a lawsuit with Enron over transactions outstanding when Enron sought bankruptcy protection.
2006-12-13: Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling is ordered to report to prison to begin serving a 24-year sentence after a judge denies his request to remain free pending appeal of his conviction.
2007-11-21: A plea agreement hearing is scheduled for three British bankers accused of embezzling $7.3 million through a Cayman Islands deal with Enron, possibly involving an admission of wrongdoing in exchange for lighter charges.
2007-11-28: The NatWest Three are due to appear before a judge for a re-arraignment hearing, on the brink of a plea agreement that could involve an admission of wrongdoing over an alleged $20m fraud related to the collapse of Enron.
2008-02-22: The "NatWest Three" bankers were sentenced to 37 months in jail each for an Enron-related fraud.
2008-04-01: Jailed former Enron boss Jeffrey Skilling launches an appeal seeking to reverse his fraud and insider trading convictions, arguing his trial in Houston was unfair.
2008-04-02: Jailed former Enron boss Jeffrey Skilling begins an appeal claiming his 24-year sentence for fraud and insider trading resulted from an unfair trial in Houston.
2009-01-06: A US appeals court upheld 19 criminal convictions against former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling but ruled that his 24-year prison sentence is too harsh and ordered him to be resentenced.
2009-10-13: The US Supreme Court agrees to hear an appeal by former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling, who is serving a 24-year prison sentence for his role in the company's 2001 collapse.
2010-03-01: The US Supreme Court hears former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling's appeal claiming his fraud trial in Houston was prejudiced by local hatred toward Enron.
2010-06-24: The US Supreme Court ruled that the "honest services" fraud law used partly to convict former Enron CEO Jeffrey Skilling was too broad, casting doubt on some of his convictions but stopping short of acquittal.
2013-06-21: Former Enron chief executive Jeffrey Skilling is resentenced to 14 years in prison after an agreement with prosecutors, reducing his original sentence of more than 24 years.
